frase_gancho.texto: Huipil, ruffled skirt, and rebozo shawl: the dress that Frida made her personal signature.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the last stop of the visit.

guion_corto.texto: Look at the embroidered huipiles, the long skirts with ruffles, and the shawls. These are garments of Mexican tradition, and the Tehuana dress, worn by the women of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, in Oaxaca, is the one most associated with Frida. For her it was not a costume. It was a way of showing her identity. Besides, the long skirt and the loose blouse naturally covered her corsets and her injured leg. Those women of the Isthmus are known for their strength and independence, and Frida admired that image. Notice the embroidery, the colors, and the flow of the fabrics. Look at how the colors are combined.

guion_largo.texto:
In these display cases there are garments that belonged to Frida. You will see embroidered blouses, long full skirts, shawls, and accessories. The museum explains that this is traditional Mexican clothing, with embroidered huipiles, long skirts, and ruffles. Among them all, the Tehuana dress is the most famous.

The Tehuana dress comes from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, in Oaxaca. It is worn by Zapotec women of that region. It has a huipil, which is a square embroidered blouse, a long full skirt, and, for festivals, a lace ruffle. The women of the Isthmus are associated with independence and trade. Frida knew about that reputation and admired it. Her mother was from Oaxaca.

To understand why Frida adopted it, we have to consider two reasons. The first is political and cultural. In the 1920s and 1930s, many artists and intellectuals wanted to revalue what was Mexican after the Revolution. Frida did so with her clothing. Wearing it was a way of showing her pride in her Mexican roots and of rejecting European fashions.

The second reason is very practical. A loose huipil and a floor-length skirt cover a corset and a thin leg very well. With those garments, attention went to her face, her jewelry, and her hairstyles with flowers.

For that reason, Frida's clothing is so important for understanding her work. In her self-portraits, the dress, the jewelry, and the hairstyle are part of the message. She does not portray herself as just any woman. She portrays herself as she wanted to be seen.

The museum has shown these pieces for years. They were part of the closed rooms, and when those were opened, people could see how much care Frida took with the way she dressed. Today the clothing on display is part of one of the best-known exhibitions about her, which has also been presented in museums in other countries.

It is helpful to know a few words. The huipil is a square blouse, sometimes embroidered with flowers. The ruffle is the strip of lace or fabric attached to the edge of the skirt. The rebozo is a long shawl worn over the shoulders or on the head. These three garments make up the dress. Frida wore it as an expression of her Mexican identity and of feminist and anti-colonialist ideas, as has also been said.

Before you leave, notice the embroidery on the huipiles. Some have large flowers, others geometric designs. Look at the colors that repeat, red, blue, and purple. Think about what it means to get dressed every day to be who you are.

texto.Origin of the dress: Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Zapotec culture
texto.Pieces: huipil, skirt with ruffle, and rebozo
texto.Clothing in the exhibition: about 300 garments, according to the museum

texto.pregunta: Myth: Frida wore traditional dresses only for her paintings and for trips abroad.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was the clothing she presented herself in. The huipiles and long skirts are part of the collection from her wardrobe that was found in the closed rooms of the house.
